source: Gomes, Selman, Kautz (1998) Boosting Combinatorial Search Through Randomization
finding: Randomised tie-breaking plus a backtrack cutoff with restarts solved hard planning, circuit and scheduling instances that the deterministic solver could not, or solved them far faster.
numbers: Deterministic vs randomised (Satz and ILOG CSP, 200MHz SGI): logistics.d 108 min to 95 s; 3bit-adder-32 over 24 h to 165 s; 3bit-adder-31 over 24 h to 17 min; round-robin 14 411 s to 250 s; round-robin 16 over 24 h to 1.4 h; round-robin 18 over 48 h to 22 h; blocks-world.d 30 min to 23 min.
limits: Cutoffs were tuned per instance by trial and error. Std dev of randomised time is about equal to the mean (geometric). Speedups are 'several orders of magnitude' only where the deterministic run did not finish at all.
agent_relevance: Restarting a stuck attempt can turn an unsolvable-in-budget task into a solvable one, if attempts differ by seed.

source: Gomes, Selman, Kautz (1998) Boosting Combinatorial Search Through Randomization
finding: There is a clear optimal cutoff, and it is far below the median run length. Too low a cutoff gives zero success; too high loses the benefit.
numbers: logistics.d cutoff table (success rate, mean cost in backtracks): cutoff 2 = 0.0, over 300,000; 4 = 0.00003, 147,816; 16 = 0.009, 1,861; 32 = 0.014, 2,405; 250 = 0.018, 13,456; 16,000 = 0.14, 107,611; 128,000 = 0.32, 307,550. Round-robin 16: best cutoff about 5e4 backtracks, expected cost 7e5 (about 1.4 h) at under 10% success per try; cutoff 1e6 gave 39% success but mean cost 2.5e6.
limits: Optimum is sharp: a 1000x change in cutoff changes mean cost by about 100x on logistics.d. Cutoff must be found per problem class.
agent_relevance: Our restart budget should be short relative to a full attempt, but not so short that no attempt can finish. Log per-attempt length and success to tune it.

source: Gomes, Selman, Kautz (1998) Boosting Combinatorial Search Through Randomization
finding: Boundary condition: blocks-world planning showed no heavy tail, and randomisation gave only a small gain there.
numbers: blocks-world.d: 30 min deterministic vs 23 min best randomised (about 1.3x). Authors say they found no heavy tails on blocks-world at any cutoff or heuristic-equivalence setting.
quote: One domain in which we have not found heavy-tails is on blocksworld planning problems.
limits: Single instance. Authors explicitly warn not every search problem gives heavy tails.
agent_relevance: Do not assume restarts help on every task. Measure the run-length spread first (G1: act on a signal).

source: Gomes, Selman, Crato, Kautz (2000) Heavy-Tailed Phenomena in Satisfiability and Constraint Satisfaction Problems
finding: Run times of randomised backtrack search on one fixed instance follow Pareto-Levy power-law tails. Hill-estimator tail indices were below 1 for all instances in their table, meaning infinite mean and variance without restarts.
numbers: Tail index alpha under 1 for all instances in Table II (quasigroup completion, round-robin, logistics, circuits). Round-robin 14 teams: 70% of runs took over 25,000 backtracks, yet about 1% took under 650.
limits: Hill estimate used the lowest 30% of the observed tail and a high cutoff (1e6) on data collection, so the tail was truncated. Fit is visual (log-log) plus estimator; no formal test against log-normal.
agent_relevance: Same prompt, same model, different seeds may give a very wide spread of outcomes. The mean is a poor summary; use quantiles.

source: Gomes, Selman, Crato, Kautz (2000) Heavy-Tailed Phenomena in Satisfiability and Constraint Satisfaction Problems
finding: Boundary conditions: heavy tails were absent for local search, for unsolvable (inconsistent) instances, and for easy solvable instances.
numbers: Figure 7: no heavy tail for local-search SAT and for unsolvable CSP instances. Over two dozen random quasigroup completion instances checked; most large solvable ones heavy-tailed, some easy ones not.
limits: Authors: heavy tail appeared for sufficiently large solvable instances needing substantial search.
agent_relevance: Restart pays on solvable-but-hard problems with high variance. On problems with no answer, restarts only waste budget; stopping rules must handle that (see Conformal Thinking, b24).

source: Luby, Sinclair, Zuckerman (1993) Optimal Speedup of Las Vegas Algorithms
finding: With a known run-time distribution the best restart strategy is a fixed cutoff. With none, the universal sequence 1,1,2,1,1,2,4,... is within a log factor of optimal, and no universal strategy can do better than a log factor.
numbers: Theorem 5: expected time of S_univ is at most 192 * ell_p * (log ell_p + 5), where ell_p is the expected time of the best fixed cutoff. Lower bound shows a log gap is unavoidable for any universal strategy.
limits: Constant 192 is a worst-case bound, far above practice. Assumes independent runs and a Las Vegas algorithm (always correct when it stops).
agent_relevance: LLM attempts are not always correct when they stop and are not independent (G4). The theorem does not transfer unchanged; use it as a schedule, not as a guarantee.

source: Huang (2007) The Effect of Restarts on the Efficiency of Clause Learning
finding: Large controlled test of restart policies in a modern clause-learning SAT solver: every restart policy beat no restarts, and Luby's was best overall, but no single policy won on every benchmark family.
numbers: TINISAT on 251 industrial instances (22 families, 2 h cutoff). Solved: no restarts 127; geometric (100,1.5) 164; fixed 700 -> 166; fixed 550 -> 168; (32,1.1) -> 174; fixed 16000 -> 178; Luby unit 32 -> 180. Total time on all instances in days: 11.28 none; 8.85; 8.49; 8.56; 8.00; 7.80; 7.68 Luby. MiniSat v1.14 solved 128 (11.45 d); Siege v4 solved 182 (7.45 d).
limits: Restarts helped here partly because the solver keeps learned clauses across restarts, so attempts are not independent. Gain is largest on satisfiable families (fvp-sat.3.0: 1 solved without restarts vs 16 with (100,1.5)).
agent_relevance: Restarts work best when what was learned is kept. For an LLM scaffold: restart the attempt, keep a short written no-good list of failed approaches (links to the no-goods subfield).

source: Huang (2007) The Effect of Restarts on the Efficiency of Clause Learning
finding: Competing view and caveat: the gap between restart policies shrinks when summed over benchmark families, because each family prefers a different policy.
numbers: Luby beat geometric (100,1.5) by only 1.2x in total time over the full set (7.68 vs 8.85 days), but by 2.5x in one detailed table. Authors say no policy is best across all families and argue a dynamic policy could gain more.
limits: Fixed decision heuristic (VSIDS variant) and fixed learning scheme; results may not transfer to other solvers.
agent_relevance: Expect policy choice to matter less than having any sane restart rule. Do not over-tune on one task family.

source: Kautz, Horvitz, Ruan, Gomes, Selman (2002) Dynamic Restart Policies
finding: Restart rules that use early signals from the run (decision-tree features of the first 1,000 solver steps) beat Luby's best fixed cutoff for known distributions.
numbers: Expected run time in choice points, dynamic n-ary vs fixed-optimal: QCP via CSP 3,295 vs 17,617 (about 5x); QCP via Satz 5,220 vs 11,959; graph colouring 8,962 vs 10,157; planning 5,099 vs 5,366. Authors report 40% to 65% gain over the Luby fixed-optimal policy.
limits: Table text was garbled in extraction; figures read from it with moderate confidence. Predictor trained on the same problem family; the observation window costs a fixed tax. Gains shrink to 3-7% on graph colouring and planning.
agent_relevance: Direct support for an impasse detector: an early-signal rule beats a fixed schedule, but only when trained on the same task family.

source: Gomes, Selman (1997) Algorithm Portfolio Design: Theory vs. Practice
finding: A portfolio of algorithms (here randomised Brelaz variants) run in parallel can beat the best single algorithm, but only when their run-time distributions cross; if one dominates everywhere, mixing only adds cost.
numbers: Quasigroup completion experiments with 10%, 20% and about 42% pre-assigned cells; portfolios for 2, 5 and 20 processors traced as mean-versus-standard-deviation (risk) frontiers. Portfolio worthwhile only if one cumulative distribution is not above the other at all points.
limits: OCR of figures poor; exact speedup factors not recovered. One structured instance family.
agent_relevance: Mixing different solvers (or prompt styles) pays only if their failures differ. With one model, failures are correlated (G4), so a portfolio gain will be smaller.

source: Lorenz (2017) Runtime Distributions and Criteria for Restarts
finding: Restarts help if and only if the run-time distribution has a suitable shape (decreasing hazard); a wrong restart strategy can be much worse than none. Scale does not matter, shape does.
numbers: Theorem 1: restarts useful iff some p in [0,1) satisfies a quantile condition (no finite mean needed). Weibull: useful for shape k<1, neutral for k=1 (exponential), harmful for k>1. Generalised Pareto k>0: useful, optimal restart time zero. Log-normal: numerical search found no useful restart for sigma below 0.48.
quote: Choosing the wrong restart strategy can result in expected runtimes which are much worse than not restarting at all.
limits: Pure theory for independent restarts; no LLM data. The sigma cut-off is numerical, not proved.
agent_relevance: Before adding restarts, check whether run lengths have a long right tail. Narrow, bell-shaped outcomes (reliable models on easy tasks) will not gain, and may lose.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Independent resampling from a weak model raises coverage (any sample correct) over four orders of magnitude, roughly log-linear in samples: an LLM version of the restart effect.
numbers: Gemma-2B on CodeContests: 0.02% with 1 sample to 7.1% with 10,000 (over 300x). Pythia-160M on MATH: 0.27% pass@1 to 57% pass@10k. SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2 via Moatless: 56% with many samples vs 43% single-attempt SOTA. Coverage fits exp(a k^b) with exceptions (Llama-3-8B on MiniF2F). Pythia on CodeContests stayed at 0 coverage at 10,000 samples.
limits: Needs a verifier (unit tests, Lean). Coverage is an upper bound, not accuracy. Fit is not exact on MiniF2F.
agent_relevance: Resample-from-scratch works when a cheap check exists. Without one, the gain is capped (see b13).

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys
finding: Boundary: without a verifier, the usual selection rules stall far below coverage.
numbers: Majority vote, reward-model best-of-N and reward-weighted vote all plateau before 100 samples on GSM8K and MATH (10,000 samples each from Llama-3-8B/70B-Instruct; ArmoRM-8B reward model). Human check of Llama-3-8B chains on GSM8K: chains almost always logically valid even on hard questions where the model got 10% or fewer samples right.
limits: Authors argue the verification gap, not the sampling, is the limit.
agent_relevance: The real cost of restarts is picking the winner. Code-run checks (G3) are what make restart schedules pay off.

source: Chen, Davis, Hanin, Bailis, Stoica, Zaharia, Zou (2024) Are More LLM Calls All You Need?
finding: More independent calls with vote or filter-then-vote is non-monotonic: it helps easy queries and hurts hard ones, so overall accuracy rises then falls.
numbers: MMLU Physics: 53% of queries easy under Vote, 47% difficult; Vote overall improves then declines with calls, Filter-Vote does the reverse (dips first). Theory gives an optimal number of calls, estimated from a small sample.
limits: Applies to voting aggregation of a single model, where the majority answer can be systematically wrong on hard items.
agent_relevance: Repetition plus vote can turn a minority-correct answer into a loser. Count agreement as a hint only (G4). Cap vote size by task difficulty.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: On MATH with PaLM 2-S*, N sequential revisions beat N parallel samples at equal budget. Easy questions favour pure sequential refinement; hard ones need a mix of sequential and parallel.
numbers: Sequential revision beats parallel best-of-N-weighted and majority at matched N (Figure 6 right). At a fixed budget an ideal sequential:parallel ratio exists. Compute-optimal allocation by difficulty matches best-of-N with up to 4x less compute (e.g. 64 vs 256 samples). Beam search wins on hard questions and low budget; best-of-N on easy and high budget.
limits: Revision model was fine-tuned for revising on MATH (not prompting only). One base model. Difficulty bins from a learned verifier.
agent_relevance: Restart vs continue is a difficulty-dependent choice. Continue first; restart when a check fails and the signal says the line is lost.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Continuing from one's own earlier answer with only a self-critique prompt does not help and often hurts; correction works only when told the truth (oracle label).
numbers: Intrinsic self-correction accuracy, standard vs round 2: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 43.0. With oracle label GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3; GPT-4 HotpotQA 49 to 59. Debate vs self-consistency on GSM8K at 6 responses: 83.2 vs 85.3; at 9: 83.0 vs 88.2.
quote: Our work shows that current LLMs struggle to self-correct their reasoning without external feedback.
limits: Page text came through a summarising fetch; tables copied as reported. Older GPT-3.5/GPT-4 models and prompts; stronger or trained models may differ.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: revise only from real output. A fresh attempt is at least as good as a self-critique loop when no check is available.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Forcing a reasoning model to continue ('Wait') raised accuracy a little and then flattened; parallel voting and tree search scaled further.
numbers: s1-32B on AIME24: 50.0% without extension to 57.6% with budget forcing twice (Wait x2). Ignoring the stop token with no string: 50.0 on AIME24, 90.2 on MATH500 vs 93.0 without. Authors state budget forcing flattens and can loop; REBASE with 16 trajectories scaled better than sequential on AIME24.
limits: One 32B model fine-tuned on 1,000 examples; 30 AIME questions, so one question is 3.3 points. Not statistically tested.
agent_relevance: Pure 'keep thinking' has a ceiling. After it, spend budget on a new attempt or an operator, not more of the same line.

source: Hassid, Synnaeve, Adi, Schwartz (2025) Don't Overthink it: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains
finding: Within one question, shorter reasoning chains are more often correct. Starting k attempts in parallel and stopping at the first finishers (a restart-like early cutoff) matches or beats majority voting at lower cost.
numbers: Shortest of k sampled chains beats a random chain by up to 18.8 points and the longest by up to 34.5 points (four reasoning models, four benchmarks); shortest chains are 50% and 67% shorter. short-1@k cuts compute by up to 40% at the same accuracy as majority voting (LN-Super-49B); short-3@k is up to 33% faster than majority@k (R1-32B, k=5) with higher accuracy.
limits: Holds within a question; across questions longer chains go with harder questions. Mainly math and GPQA-D.
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM analogue of a cutoff: a chain still running long is a signal it lost the thread. A length-based abort and restart is a cheap, code-checked rule.

source: OPPO AI Agent Team (2025) Scaling Test-time Compute for LLM Agents
finding: On a multi-step agent benchmark, parallel best-of-N helped most; reflection (revision) did not help overall and its value depended on when it was triggered.
numbers: Baseline agent score 55.76; always-on reflection 55.15 overall; reflection gave Level 1 71.7 vs 66.04 but hurt Level 2 (51.16 vs 58.14). Threshold-triggered reflection: threshold <8 gave 53.33, <5 gave 52.12, <2 gave 56.36. BoN gave about an eight-point gain over baseline; beam search and DVTS gave no clear gain.
limits: GPT-4.1 agent on one benchmark with small level subsets; tables partly garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Fits G1: revise on a signal, not on a schedule. Rare, well-triggered reflection beats frequent reflection.

source: Anonymous (2026) LLM-Driven Heuristic Synthesis for Industrial Process Control: Lessons from Hot Steel Rolling
finding: Direct test of Luby restarts on an LLM search loop (Gemini 2.5 Pro, fresh context per sub-run). Moderate-length runs match the hindsight-optimal allocation, and Luby reaches that regime without hindsight.
numbers: 52 ad-hoc runs (730 iterations): best reward 55.5, found by one run. Luby unit 5, 15 sub-runs, 160 iterations: unseeded best 51.6 in 4.1 h vs 27 h; seeded best 48.3 but higher median (43.2 vs 34.4 unseeded). Luby needs 1.1 to 1.8x the iterations of the best fixed cutoff to reach reward targets; unit 1 costs 2.8x. The campaign sat at the 39th percentile of 20,000 simulated campaigns. Runs of 30 iterations under-performed at matched budget; 1-iteration sampling and very long runs fell behind.
limits: One domain, one model, one real campaign; gap 51.6 vs 55.5 not tested for significance. Best heuristic came from a single lucky run.
agent_relevance: Best in-domain support: restart with a reset context on a Luby schedule with unit about 5 iterations; keep best-so-far.

source: Anonymous (2026) LLM-Driven Heuristic Synthesis for Industrial Process Control
finding: Depth and restart both matter: in 14 of 15 Luby sub-runs the best heuristic came from a later iteration (typically iterations 3 to 9), so continuing inside a run mattered; one sub-run's lucky first draft (50.0) beat later refinement.
numbers: 14 of 15 sub-runs best at iteration 3-9. Out-of-distribution test (42 cases): Luby pool of 156 heuristics: best single 51.2, K=4 portfolio 59.9, oracle 67.3; ad-hoc pool of 18: 41.8, 58.7, 63.6.
limits: Pool sizes differ (156 vs 18), so the pool comparison is confounded with sample count.
agent_relevance: Continue for a few iterations, then restart. Restart-every-time loses depth; never-restart loses lucky starts.

source: Qi et al. (2025) Optimizing Anytime Reasoning via Budget Relative Policy Optimization
finding: Anytime property for LLM reasoning: truncate the thinking at sampled budgets, force a summary answer, and reward each; this beats standard end-reward training at all budgets in math reasoning.
numbers: Abstract-level claim: AnytimeReasoner with BRPO outperforms GRPO across thinking budgets and prior distributions, with better training efficiency; exact point gains not recorded here.
limits: Needs RL training, so it does not apply to a scaffold-only agent; math tasks only.
agent_relevance: Shows answer-at-any-stop can be measured. Our agent can force a best-so-far answer in every state (G6) and log quality versus budget.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Budget-Aware Anytime Reasoning with LLM-Synthesized Preference Data
finding: Defines an Anytime Index (quality per token across budgets) and tests it on NaturalPlan Trip, AIME and GPQA across Grok-3, GPT-oss, GPT-4.1/4o and LLaMA-3.3.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read; the headline gain size was cut off and is not recorded.
limits: Only the first page was read. Treat as a metric proposal, not a confirmed effect size.
agent_relevance: A ready metric for our harness: area under quality-versus-tokens, reported with every arm.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget
finding: Stopping rules framed as risk control: an upper confidence threshold stops when confident, and a lower threshold stops unsolvable instances early; thresholds are set on a validation set to cap error rate.
numbers: Introduction read: two risk types (stop too early on a wrong confident answer; give up on a solvable item). No effect sizes recorded.
limits: Only the first page was read. Calibration needs a validation set per domain.
agent_relevance: The abort side of a restart schedule: a give-up rule for unsolvable items so budget is not burned (G6).

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
finding: Sampling many chains and taking the majority answer beats a single greedy chain; gains are large on arithmetic and smaller on commonsense.
numbers: Abstract only: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 points over greedy chain-of-thought.
limits: Only the abstract page was read, so not marked opened. Chains come from one model, so errors correlate.
agent_relevance: Baseline for restart as independent resampling plus vote; weaker than check-based selection.

source: Kautz et al. (2002) Dynamic Restart Policies: mixed-distribution theory
finding: With mixed run-time distributions and no per-run observation, the best fixed cutoff can be no cutoff at all; with a good predictor, the best policy changes.
numbers: Worked case: if a run ends in 10 or 100 steps with equal probability, always restart after 10; if instances come from different distributions the best fixed cutoff can be none. Proposition 1: with no observations the optimal policy is the optimal fixed cutoff.
limits: Stylised theory example, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: A restart rule needs a signal that separates easy from hard instances; otherwise tune one cutoff on pooled data.
